facts.statehood_note: Admitted as a free state when President James Buchanan signed the admission bill.
facts.motto: Ad astra per aspera (To the stars through difficulties)
facts.name_origin: Named for the Kansas River, which was named for the Kansa (Kaw) people, the "People of the Southwind."

government.legislature: Kansas Legislature (meets every year in Topeka at the Kansas State Capitol)
government.chambers: Kansas Senate (40 members, 4-year terms) and Kansas House of Representatives (125 members, 2-year terms)
government.executive: Governor and lieutenant governor, elected by the people to 4-year terms; no one may be elected governor more than two terms in a row. Other elected executive officers include the secretary of state and attorney general.
government.courts: Kansas Supreme Court (7 justices, 6-year terms; the governor appoints from a nominating commission's list), Kansas Court of Appeals (14 judges), and district courts in 31 judicial districts.
government.constitution: The Wyandotte Constitution, signed July 29, 1859, and approved by voters on October 4, 1859 (10,421 to 5,530). It made Kansas a free state, set its western border, and is still the state constitution, with many amendments.
government.kid_line: "There shall be no slavery in this state" (Kansas Constitution, Bill of Rights, Section 6).

long_ago.about: In the 1540s the Wichita lived around the great bend of the Arkansas River in central Kansas, in large cone-shaped houses thatched with grass. They farmed corn, pumpkins, and tobacco, hunted bison, and traded extra corn to neighbors.

The Kaw, the "People of the Southwind," settled along the Missouri River in present-day Doniphan County in the later 1600s. By the mid-1700s they were the main nation in most of northern and eastern Kansas.

The Kitkahahki (Republican) band of the Pawnee built a large village of earth lodges in present-day Republic County in the late 1700s and early 1800s. Remains of 22 earth lodges and storage pits are still there.
The Osage are one of the nations native to Kansas. In an 1825 treaty they gave up land that became nearly all of Kansas and Oklahoma and kept a reservation in southern Kansas.
These Plains nations are also counted among the peoples native to the land that is now Kansas.

today.about: Federally recognized nation headquartered near Mayetta; the Potawatomi moved to present-day Kansas in 1846.
Federally recognized nation headquartered in Horton, with its reservation in Brown County; the Kickapoo were granted land there in 1832.

today.nation: Iowa Tribe of Kansas and Nebraska
today.about: Federally recognized nation headquartered in White Cloud; its reservation spans Brown and Doniphan counties in Kansas and Richardson County, Nebraska.

today.nation: Sac and Fox Nation of Missouri in Kansas and Nebraska
today.about: Federally recognized nation headquartered in Reserve, Kansas, near the Nebraska line.

first_peoples.today_note: Four reservations remain in Kansas (Iowa, Kickapoo, Potawatomi, and Sac and Fox). Many nations once in Kansas now live in Oklahoma: the Kaw Nation (over 3,100 members) is headquartered in Kaw City, the Wichita and Affiliated Tribes in Anadarko, and the Osage Nation, whose people had mostly left Kansas by 1870, in Pawhuska. None of these three nations has a reservation in Kansas today. Native people of many nations also live in Kansas cities and towns.
sites: Pawnee Indian Museum State Historic Site, Republic County (museum built in 1967 around an earth lodge floor, with artifacts left in place)
Allegawaho Memorial Heritage Park near Council Grove (the last Kaw village in Kansas, being restored by the Kaw Nation)

history.event: Spanish explorer Francisco Vázquez de Coronado reaches Quivira, the Wichita homeland near present-day Great Bend. He finds grass lodges, not the gold he wanted.
The Kaw (Kansa) settle along the Missouri River in present-day Doniphan County.
The Kitkahahki band of the Pawnee build an earth lodge village in present-day Republic County.
The United States claims most of present-day Kansas in the Louisiana Purchase.
William Becknell's traders open the Santa Fe Trail to trade with Mexico; about two-thirds of the 750-mile trail crosses Kansas.
In a treaty signed in St. Louis, the Osage give up land that becomes nearly all of Kansas and Oklahoma. Kaw treaties with the U.S. in 1825, 1846, and 1859 bring hunger and disease to the Kaw.

The U.S. forces eastern nations west. The Delaware are the first to sign a treaty for land in Kansas, and nearly 30 nations, including the Shawnee, Potawatomi, Kickapoo, and Wyandot, are given land here.

The Kansas-Nebraska Act (May 30) creates Kansas Territory. Fighting between Free-State and proslavery settlers becomes known as Bleeding Kansas, and nations moved here are pushed off their land again.
Proslavery forces sack the Free-State town of Lawrence on May 21. Free-State fighters take revenge in the Pottawatomie Massacre on May 24.
Voters approve the Wyandotte Constitution on October 4, making Kansas a free state.
Kansas becomes the 34th state on January 29, 1861, as a free state, months before the Civil War begins.
On October 28, the First Kansas Colored Infantry fights at Island Mound, Missouri, the first Black soldiers in the Union army tested in battle.
On August 21, William Quantrill's Confederate raiders attack Lawrence. They destroy more than 200 homes and businesses and leave 150 men dead or dying.
The Kaw are removed to Indian Territory (Oklahoma) in 1873. In 1877, Black families from the Lexington, Kentucky, area found the town of Nicodemus.

trailblazers.name: Clarina I. H. Nichols
trailblazers.group: White woman, women's rights leader and abolitionist
trailblazers.text: Nichols spoke to the delegates at the 1859 Wyandotte Convention for the Moneka Woman's Rights Association. Thanks to her work, the Kansas Constitution protected married women's property rights, mothers' child custody rights, and equal rights in public schools.

trailblazers.name: Benjamin "Pap" Singleton
trailblazers.group: Black American man, freedom seeker and community founder
trailblazers.text: Born enslaved in Tennessee, Singleton escaped and later helped other freedom seekers in Detroit. After the Civil War he urged freed people to buy land in Kansas and organized colonies there, earning the name "Father of the Negro Exodus."

trailblazers.name: Charles Curtis
trailblazers.text: Curtis spent part of his childhood on the Kaw Reservation near Council Grove and became the first American Indian vice president of the United States (1929–1933). He also wrote the Curtis Act of 1898, which weakened tribal governments and broke up shared tribal lands, harming many Native nations.

trailblazers.name: Amelia Earhart
trailblazers.text: Born in Atchison, Earhart became the first woman to cross the Atlantic by air (as a passenger in 1928). In 1932 she set a record flying solo across the Atlantic, was elected president of the Ninety-Nines, a group of women pilots, and in 1937 vanished while trying to fly around the world.

trailblazers.name: Langston Hughes
trailblazers.text: Hughes spent much of his childhood in Lawrence and Topeka, living with his grandmother in Lawrence. He became a leading writer of the Harlem Renaissance, and his first published poem, "The Negro Speaks of Rivers" (1921), became his signature work.

trailblazers.name: Gordon Parks
trailblazers.group: Black American man, photographer and filmmaker
trailblazers.text: Born in Fort Scott, Parks bought a used camera at a pawn shop and became a staff photographer for Life magazine. He wrote the novel The Learning Tree and directed its 1969 film version, and he also directed Shaft.

trailblazers.name: Hazel Gomez
trailblazers.text: Gomez spent her life serving people in need in Topeka. At 18 she helped organize the Y-Señoritas club at the Topeka YWCA, and she was a founding member of Topeka's chapter of the League of United Latin American Citizens (LULAC), later serving two terms as its state president. In 1973 she became the first chairperson of the advisory board for the LULAC Elderly Center.

landforms: Mount Sunflower (highest point, about 4,039 feet, Wallace County)
waters: Missouri River (part of the northeast border)
geography.regions: The Kansas Geological Survey divides Kansas into 11 physiographic regions, including the flat High Plains in the west, the Smoky Hills and Red Hills in the middle, the Flint Hills, and the Osage Cuestas, Glaciated Region, and Ozark Plateau in the east.

ecosystems.name: Tallgrass prairie (Flint Hills)
ecosystems.about: Less than 4% of North America's tallgrass prairie remains, and most of it is in the Kansas Flint Hills. In 2009, 13 bison were brought to Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve, and the herd has grown to about 90.

ecosystems.name: Wetlands (Cheyenne Bottoms)
ecosystems.about: Cheyenne Bottoms is one of the top stopover places in the U.S. for migrating shorebirds, and it is a Wetland of International Importance. Ten shorebird species have a large share of their populations stop there in a year.

science.weather: Kansas has severe thunderstorms with large hail, flash floods, damaging winds, and extreme summer heat. It averages more than 50 tornadoes a year.
science.resources: Nearly 90% of Kansas land is farmland. Wheat is the leading crop (about 40% of U.S. winter wheat), along with corn, sorghum, soybeans, and cattle; Wichita is a major airplane-building center, and wind energy is another important industry.
science.highlight: About 80 million years ago, a shallow sea (the Western Interior Seaway) covered Kansas. Its chalk forms Monument Rocks, about 70 feet tall and full of fossils, and Kansas has named the flying reptile Pteranodon its state flying fossil and the sea reptile Tylosaurus its state marine fossil.

g3_ss.title: Kansas Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Kansas, Topeka, and Wichita on a map, learn the symbols (sunflower, meadowlark, bison), and compare the Legislature, governor, and courts to jobs in a community.

g3_ss.title: Kansas First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Meet the Wichita, Kaw, and Pawnee through their homes (grass lodges and earth lodges), then learn about the four nations with reservations in Kansas today.

g3_ss.title: Kansas Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Read short stories of Amelia Earhart, Gordon Parks, Langston Hughes, and Pap Singleton, and make a trailblazer card for each.

g45_ss.title: Kansas First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Study the Wichita, Kaw, Pawnee, and Osage, the 1825 treaties, and how nearly 30 eastern nations were forced into Kansas and then pushed out again after 1854.

g45_ss.title: Spanish Explorers and the Santa Fe Trail
g45_ss.plan: Follow Coronado's 1541 trip to Quivira and the 1821 Santa Fe Trail to see how Kansas connected Native nations, Mexico, and the United States.

g45_ss.title: Bleeding Kansas to Nicodemus (1854–1877)
g45_ss.plan: Trace the fight over slavery, the Wyandotte Constitution, statehood as a free state, the First Kansas Colored Infantry, Quantrill's raid, Kaw removal, and the founding of Nicodemus.

g3_sci.title: Prairie Plants and Animals
g3_sci.plan: Explore the tallgrass prairie of the Flint Hills and why bison were brought back to it.

g3_sci.title: Wild Kansas Weather
g3_sci.plan: Learn how thunderstorms, hail, and tornadoes form and practice tornado safety steps.

g3_sci.title: Birds on the Move
g3_sci.plan: Use Cheyenne Bottoms to learn why shorebirds stop at wetlands during migration.

g45_sci.title: When Kansas Was a Sea
g45_sci.plan: Use Monument Rocks chalk and fossils like Pteranodon and Tylosaurus to learn how rock layers record an ancient sea.

g45_sci.title: Landforms of Kansas
g45_sci.plan: Map the 11 physiographic regions, from the High Plains to the Flint Hills, and compare their rocks and land shapes.

g45_sci.title: Farming the Plains
g45_sci.plan: Study wheat, soil, and water, and how Kansas farms and wind energy use natural resources.
